clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant red cell membrane cation-leak disorder in which red cells are dehydrated (xerocytes), most often from gain-of-function variants in PIEZO1 (a mechanosensitive cation channel) and less commonly KCNN4 (the Gardos channel)
Causes a compensated or mild to moderate haemolytic anaemia with a characteristically raised MCHC and increased reticulocytes; the film may show few overt stomatocytes but target and desiccated cells
Iron overload is common and can occur out of proportion to transfusion, sometimes as the presenting problem, mimicking hereditary haemochromatosis
Perinatal oedema, transient hydrops fetalis or ascites is a recognised feature of PIEZO1-related disease and may resolve spontaneously
Splenectomy is contraindicated: it does not reliably correct the anaemia and carries a high risk of subsequent venous thromboembolism, including portal and pulmonary thrombosis
Osmotic fragility is typically decreased because the dehydrated cells resist osmotic lysis, and osmotic gradient ektacytometry shows a characteristic left-shifted curve
The overlapping and heterogeneous stomatocytosis syndromes require careful characterisation, since management, particularly avoidance of splenectomy, hinges on correct classification
reference.pathophysiology: Dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis is caused by dominant gain-of-function variants in red cell membrane cation channels, chiefly PIEZO1 (a mechanosensitive non-selective cation channel) and occasionally KCNN4 (the calcium-activated Gardos potassium channel). Abnormal channel gating produces a net cation leak in which potassium loss exceeds sodium gain, so intracellular monovalent cation and water content fall and the cell becomes dehydrated with an increased haemoglobin concentration. The resulting rigid, poorly deformable red cells have a shortened lifespan and undergo haemolysis, while disordered iron regulation with relative hepcidin suppression promotes parenchymal iron loading independent of transfusion.
additionalDifferentials: Overhydrated hereditary stomatocytosis and other stomatocytosis variants
Hereditary haemochromatosis, when the iron-overload phenotype dominates
Other causes of a raised MCHC, such as cold agglutinins or sample artefact
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with MCHC (raised) and reticulocyte count
Blood film for stomatocytes, target cells and desiccated forms
Osmotic gradient ektacytometry, showing a characteristic left-shifted curve where available
Iron studies with hepatic iron quantification by MRI (T2* or R2*)
Molecular testing of PIEZO1 and KCNN4 with family segregation studies
Exclusion of HFE and other haemochromatosis genes when iron loading dominates
redFlags: Perinatal hydrops fetalis, ascites or unexplained oedema
Progressive iron overload with hepatic or cardiac dysfunction
Venous or arterial thrombosis, especially after prior splenectomy
reference.prognosis: The haemolytic anaemia is usually mild and compatible with a normal lifespan, but iron overload and thrombotic complications, particularly after splenectomy, drive long-term morbidity. Outcomes are good when splenectomy is avoided and iron status is monitored and treated.
pitfalls: Performing splenectomy, which is contraindicated and carries a high thrombotic risk
Misattributing iron overload solely to transfusion or to primary haemochromatosis
Missing the diagnosis because stomatocytes are sparse on the film
Confusing it with overhydrated stomatocytosis, which behaves differently
Overlooking the dominant family history and perinatal oedema as diagnostic clues
management: Avoid splenectomy, which fails to correct the anaemia and markedly increases the risk of venous, portal and pulmonary thrombosis
Folic acid supplementation to support chronic compensated haemolysis
Regular monitoring of iron status with hepatic iron quantification, treating iron overload with iron chelation or cautious venesection even in the absence of transfusion
Reserve red-cell transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, which is usually mild and only infrequently required
Thromboprophylaxis and a low threshold for investigating venous thromboembolism given the intrinsic prothrombotic tendency
Foetal and perinatal surveillance for hydrops, effusions or ascites in PIEZO1-related disease, with supportive care as these often resolve spontaneously
Genetic counselling and molecular testing of PIEZO1 and KCNN4 with family segregation studies, given autosomal dominant inheritance
